entries.subject: VLT/MATISSE February 2020 pseudo-continuum visibilities, JMMC OiDB
entries.finding: 29 calibrated files from 8 and 19 February 2020 (stations A0-B2-D0-C1 and K0-G2-D0-J3) are public in the OiDB at calibration level 3. Averaged over beam-commuter repeats in the paper's pseudo-continuum windows they give 780 squared visibilities and 520 closure phases. A uniform-disc fit gives 42.45 mas; the paper reports 43.8 mas for this epoch. The night of 25 February (A0-G1-J2-J3) is also public but was not used by the paper and is not used here.

entries.subject: Image reconstruction with SQUEEZE versus the published IRBIS image
entries.finding: The public SQUEEZE code at a pinned commit, with the paper's prior and hyperparameter, gives a near-uniform disc (maximum over median inside the disc 1.30 after the 4 mas beam) that fits the data at reduced chi-squared 0.35 on squared visibilities and 1.12 on closure phases, and looks like the paper's February 2020 panel. Three settings (entropy 10 and 1, total variation 1) agree with one another. The dataset casts the entropy-10 image convolved to the 4 mas beam; the raw posterior mean is retained as a document. An earlier hand-written solver in the pilot produced a bright western limb at two to four times the median with every prior; it was an artefact of that solver and is not used. Negating every closure phase fits equally well (1.30 against 1.28) and correlates best with the image rotated by 180 degrees, so the handedness of the faint asymmetry is weakly constrained.

entries.subject: SiO (2-0) band 4.004-4.012 um as a second dataset
entries.finding: The ESO pipeline flags every channel above 4.001 um in the pinned files. Using the flagged channels anyway, SQUEEZE fits their squared visibilities (reduced chi-squared 1.2 with visibilities alone) but not their closure phases: 25.6 as delivered, 24.8 with every phase negated, 23.5 on a 100 mas field. The paper shows an SiO image from the same nights, so either its reduction kept channels the archive flags or its closure-phase errors were inflated. Not shipped.
entries.revisitWhen: A reduction that keeps the SiO channels unflagged, or a stated closure-phase error model, fits them at reduced chi-squared near 1.

entries.subject: December 2018 and December 2020 MATISSE epochs; PIONIER 2014, GRAVITY 2019-2023, AMBER 2006-2018, ALMA 2015 and 2023
entries.finding: The December 2018 and December 2020 MATISSE epochs are cast as datasets matisse-2018-12 and matisse-2020-12 from the 111 and 48 calibrated OiDB files of Drevon et al.'s collection, with the February 2020 recipe; neither passes the reconstruction check (see the README), so their patches are labelled unconfirmed. The ESO archive also holds raw PIONIER, GRAVITY and AMBER frames and ALMA six public projects, which each need their pipeline run first. Revisit when: a raw-pipeline epoch that passes the reconstruction check.

entries.subject: VLT/SPHERE/ZIMPOL images (ESO Phase 3 collection BETELGEUSE-B, December 2024)
entries.finding: The public V-band polarimetric product resolves the disc at about 14 pixels of 3.6 mas with a 16 mas beam: three resolution elements. Not a surface. The deep H-alpha products of the same collection are the companion search, with the star subtracted; their detection map is kept as a sidebar picture (see companion-siwarha).
entries.revisitWhen: A public image of the photosphere with at least ten resolution elements across the disc.

entries.subject: Rotation-axis inclination
entries.finding: ALMA gives the pole position angle, 48.0 +/- 3.5 degrees, and P/sin i; the inclination is not measured. Hubble spectra (Uitenbroek et al. 1998) suggested the pole points about 20 degrees from the line of sight. The pole is placed in the plane of the sky; a measured inclination would tilt the sphere and move the photographed hemisphere's latitude.
entries.revisitWhen: A published inclination with a stated method.

entries.subject: Distance
entries.finding: Joyce et al. (2020) 168 (+27/-15) pc is adopted; it agrees with the Hipparcos parallax (153 pc, van Leeuwen 2007) and with the interferometric radius, and differs from the radio astrometric 222 pc of Harper et al. (2017). The choice moves the physical radius by 40 percent and nothing else in the scene.

entries.subject: Whether the MATISSE reconstruction's bright and dark patches beat a spotless disc across plausible disc sizes
entries.finding: Run through image-star.mts with --calibrated on the 29 pinned files, the season merges byte-identically to the pinned continuum OIFITS and SQUEEZE fits it at reduced chi-squared 0.31 and 1.20; its patches come back from two interleaved halves (correlation 0.57, limit 0.5). Spotless twins at 0.98 to 1.02 times the fitted 43.08 mas leave patch maps at 0.49 to 0.81 of the image's strength (spot ratios 2.02 to 1.24, limit 2); the twin of 42.45 mas this dataset was first checked with gave 2.73. On one half of the data, twins between 42.0 and 44.3 mas range from rms 0.03 to 0.14 against the image's 0.13, and 10 000 iterations, four chains or half-size pixels did not make a spotty twin clean. π¹ Gruis's twins stay clean over the same relative range. The dataset is kept by the user's decision and its notes say the patches are not confirmed.
entries.revisitWhen: A reconstruction of these or more data (the public 25 February 2020 night, another recipe or another code) whose spotless twins stay clean across ±2 percent in size, or a published spotless-disc test of the MATISSE images.

entries.subject: Limb darkening
entries.finding: The disc is dimmed toward the limb by the quadratic law Neilson & Lester (2013), A&A 554, A98 compute from spherical ATLAS (SATLAS) model atmospheres for the Johnson V band at 3,600 K and log g -0.08 for 17.75 solar masses (u1 1.114, u2 -0.025); the model atmosphere is extended, and the law reaches zero at 99.6% of the radius, where the disc is drawn dark: a model, because no fit of this star's limb is used. Gravity: log g from the mass and radius in packages/astronomy/data/bodies/betelgeuse.json: -0.079.

entries.subject: How far toward the limb the reconstructions are cast onto the sphere
entries.finding: Until 2026-10-03 the images were cast only to 70 degrees from the disc centre, so the drawn disc ended at 0.94 of the radius in a toothed edge and 5.3 to 8.9 percent of each image's light was left off it. They are now cast to 88 degrees and cover 48.5 percent of the sphere. A first cast at 88 degrees left holes in the last pixel of the disc, because the shared footprint asked each of the four pixels around a point for a surface point of its own and the ones beyond the silhouette have none; a reconstruction is a brightness field over its whole frame, so its frames are now sampled at the point itself, held to the limit by the point's own normal (sampleSkyField).

entries.subject: The light between the disc edge and one beam outside it (1.00 to 1.19 stellar radii)
entries.finding: Measured on the beam-convolved images about each one's centroid, with the disc at 42.45 mas: this zone holds 7.5, 9.6 and 9.8 percent of the light in December 2018, February 2020 and December 2020, at about a fifth of the peak brightness; beyond it lie 0.6, 10.3 and 0.9 percent. It is the star's own edge smeared by the beam. Drawing it on the off-limb volume's scale was composed face-on from the images before any bake: that scale tops out at 6 percent of the central brightness, so the zone becomes a flat saturated band, and in December 2018 and 2020 the band and scattered reconstruction noise would be the whole volume. So the off-limb volume keeps starting one beam out, only February 2020 has one, and the gap is stated in the README.
entries.revisitWhen: One display scale that carries both the photosphere's patches and the faint light outside it.

entries.subject: Siwarha (Alpha Orionis B), the companion: orbit, detection and nature
entries.finding: Drawn as a point on its orbit, an astronomy record with no package: no paper measures its size or temperature. Period, orbit size, transit time and circular shape are the radial-velocity fit of MacLeod et al. (2025); the inclination is their astrometric fit. The orbit's direction on the sky is the position angle at which VLT/SPHERE detected the companion on 6 December 2024 (Montarges et al. 2026: 52.32 +/- 0.18 mas, 117.12 +/- 0.60 degrees, 6.1 sigma), a quarter of a period after the 2023 transit; MacLeod et al.'s astrometric node of 60 +/- 6 degrees does not pass through it and is not used. The recorded orbit puts the companion 46.1 mas from the star at 113.6 degrees that night. Its mass is disputed (0.60 +/- 0.14 solar masses at least from the radial velocities; 2.6 to 3.1 as a coeval star; under about 1.5 from the far ultraviolet; or reflected light at a bow shock), so the minimum mass is recorded and no sphere is drawn. ESO's Phase 3 collection BETELGEUSE-B publishes the detection's signal-to-noise map, which is shown in the sidebar as a picture because one point of light cannot be laid onto a surface. The IAU adopted the name on 22 September 2025.
entries.revisitWhen: A second epoch that confirms it is bound, or a measured color or size: it then becomes a body with its own package.
